content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines on mental health in the workplace, emphasizing the importance of creating safe, healthy, and inclusive work environments. These guidelines are available in both electronic and print formats, with specific ISBNs for each version. The publication is copyrighted by WHO in 2022, and certain rights are reserved under a Creative Commons license. Users are permitted to copy, redistribute, and adapt the work for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, a disclaimer must be included, stating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation. The guidelines stress that working individuals, regardless of their employment type, have an inherent right to the highest attainable standard of mental health at work. People living with mental health conditions are entitled to access, participate in, and thrive in the workplace. Governments and employers are responsible for ensuring that work environments prevent excessive stress and mental health risks, protect and promote mental well-being, and support individuals in participating fully and effectively in the workforce without stigma, discrimination, or abuse. The workplace is undergoing significant changes due to factors such as technology, globalization, demographic shifts, emergencies, and climate change. The COVID-19 pandemic has further disrupted labor markets, accelerating changes in remote work, e-commerce, and automation. These shifts have created new pressures and exacerbated existing stresses, potentially undermining workers' mental health. Addressing mental health in the workplace is essential for preparing for the future of work and adapting to a changing world. Managing mental health at work, while challenging, should not be viewed as burdensome. Instead, it presents an opportunity for growth and sustainable development. Safe, healthy, and inclusive workplaces not only improve mental and physical health but also reduce absenteeism, enhance work performance and productivity, boost staff morale and motivation, and minimize conflicts among colleagues. Good mental health enables individuals to cope with life’s stresses, realize their abilities, learn and work effectively, and contribute actively to their communities. Conversely, favorable working conditions help protect mental health. The guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for interventions to prevent, protect, promote, and support workers' mental health. They highlight the importance of organizational interventions, training for managers and workers, and individual-focused strategies. Special attention is given to workers with mental health conditions, offering interventions to help them gain employment, return to work after an absence, or receive reasonable accommodations in the workplace. WHO is committed to supporting member states in promoting and protecting workers' mental health. The Comprehensive Mental Health Action Plan 2013–2030 underscores the need for countries to foster safe, supportive, and decent working conditions for all. Additionally, the WHO Global Strategy on Health, Environment, and Climate Change identifies workplaces as critical settings for preventing modifiable risks, particularly for non-communicable diseases. These guidelines represent a milestone in leveraging workplaces as platforms for action, providing a framework for evidence-based measures to ensure effective prevention, promotion, and support for mental health at work. The mental health of workers is integral to the wealth of enterprises and societies across all countries and sectors. Governments, enterprises, and stakeholders in the world of work are encouraged to implement these guidelines as a tool for creating safe, healthy, and inclusive workplaces that promote and protect mental health. The development of these guidelines was led by the WHO Department of Mental Health and Substance Use and the Department of Health, Environment, and Climate Change, under the leadership of Dévora Kestel and Maria Neira. The technical officer responsible for the guidelines was Aiysha Malik. Contributions were made by a WHO Steering Group, chaired by Mark van Ommeren, and various technical experts, consultants, and external reviewers. WHO also acknowledges the input of the International Labour Organization (ILO) and other key stakeholders. The guidelines were informed by extensive evidence reviews and synthesis conducted by teams from institutions worldwide.
